questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Shortest Distance Between an Osculating Plane and the Origin
questions.problem:
Find the shortest distance between the origin and the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ T(t) & =⟨0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ N(t) & =⟨0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩=⟨0,0,1⟩ \\ N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩=⟨0,-1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is

$$
p=r(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨2,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩=⟨2,1,0⟩.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(\frac{\pi }{2})$ and the principal normal $N(\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =T(\frac{\pi }{2})\times N(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =⟨0,0,1⟩\times ⟨0,-1,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =i \\  & =⟨1,0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
d=\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=|p\cdot n|,
$$

since $‖n‖=1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|p\cdot n| \\  & =|⟨2,1,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,0,0⟩| \\  & =|2+0+0| \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the shortest distance between the origin and the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{3}$, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,\,4t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t⟩ \\ T(t) & =\frac{1}{5}⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,\,4,\,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t⟩ \\ N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,\,0,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡3t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{3}$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\frac{1}{5}⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}),\,4,\,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3})⟩=\frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,3⟩ \\ N(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}),\,0,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3})⟩=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{3}$ is

$$
p=r(\frac{\pi }{3})=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}),\,4(\frac{\pi }{3}),\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3})⟩=⟨-1,\frac{4\pi }{3},0⟩.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(\frac{\pi }{3})$ and the principal normal $N(\frac{\pi }{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =T(\frac{\pi }{3})\times N(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,3⟩\times ⟨1,0,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 4 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\,j-4\,k) \\  & =⟨0,\frac{3}{5},-\frac{4}{5}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
d=\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=|p\cdot n|,
$$

since $‖n‖=1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|p\cdot n| \\  & =|⟨-1,\frac{4\pi }{3},0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\frac{3}{5},-\frac{4}{5}⟩| \\  & =|\,0+\frac{4\pi }{3}\cdot \frac{3}{5}+0\,| \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits Along Different Paths for Multivariable Functions
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}
$$

- The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=x$
- The limit evaluates to $2$ along the path $y={x}^{2}$
- The limit exists and is equal to $2$
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}=\frac{2\cdot {0}^{2}}{2\cdot {0}^{2}-0}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{x(2x-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2x}{2x-1} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 0}{2\cdot 0-1} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is also true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y={x}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{2}}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}=\text{DNE}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{2y+x}{3x+y}
$$

- The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=x$
- The limit evaluates to $-\frac{1}{2}$ along the path $y=-x$
- The limit exists and is equal to $0$
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{2y+x}{3x+y}=\frac{2\cdot 0+0}{3\cdot 0+0}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is false. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\frac{2y+x}{3x+y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2x+x}{3x+x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{3x}{4x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=-x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=-x}\frac{2y+x}{3x+y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{-2x+x}{3x-x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{-x}{2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{2y+x}{3x+y}=\text{DNE}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Using Differentials to Approximate the Change in a Multivariable Function
questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y,$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y)$ from $(0,e)$ to $(1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,\text{d}x+\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(0,e),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(0,e) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡e\,\text{d}x+\frac{0}{e}\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(0+Δx,e+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈1\,Δx+0\,Δy.
$$

Moving from $(0,e)$ to $(1,2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1-0=1, \\ Δy & =2-e.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\,Δx+0\,Δy \\  & ≈1\cdot (1)+0\cdot (2-e) \\  & ≈1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ increases by approximately $1.$

questions.problem: If $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y,$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y)$ from $(0.5,1)$ to $(0,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2x\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(0.5,1),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(0.5,1) & =2\cdot 0.5\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+1\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(0.5+Δx,1+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈1\,Δx+1\,Δy.
$$

Moving from $(0.5,1)$ to $(0,2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =0-0.5=-0.5, \\ Δy & =2-1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\,Δx+1\,Δy \\  & ≈1\cdot (-0.5)+1\cdot (1) \\  & ≈0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ increases by approximately $0.5.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Plane of a Surface Given Implicitly Using the Gradient Vector
questions.problem: Consider the surface ${2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}=2.$ Given that $n=⟨a,b,c⟩$ is a non-zero normal vector to the surface at the point $(1,-1,1),$ what is the value of $\frac{c}{b}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's define  $f(x,y,z)={2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=2.$  

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy})j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy})k \\  & =({2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}\cdot 2y\operatorname{ln}⁡2)i+({2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}\cdot 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡2)j+({2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}\cdot 6z\operatorname{ln}⁡2)k \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2(y\,\text{ }{2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}\text{ }i+x\,\text{ }{2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}\text{ }j+3z\,\text{ }{2}^{3{z}^{2}+2xy}\text{ }k) \\ ∇f(1,-1,1) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2((-1)\cdot \text{ }{2}^{3(1)^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot (-1)}\text{ }i+1\cdot \,\text{ }{2}^{3(1)^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot (-1)}\text{ }j+3(1)\cdot {2}^{3(1)^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot (-1)}\text{ }k) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2(-{2}^{1}\text{ }i+{2}^{1}\text{ }j+3\cdot {2}^{1}\text{ }k) \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡2(-i+j+3\text{ }k) \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,4\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,12\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩=⟨-4\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,4\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,12\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩.$

Finally, $\frac{c}{b}=\frac{12\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Reconstructing a Three-Variable Function From Its Gradient
questions.problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,i+2yz\,j+{y}^{2}\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2yz\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int (2yz)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={y}^{2}z+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)={y}^{2}z+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{y}^{2}z+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z) & ={y}^{2} \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{y}^{2}z+C.
$$

questions.problem: Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ where $F(x,y,z)=(y+1)\,i+(x+z+1)\,j+(y+1)\,k.$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+z+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+1
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (y+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =xy+x+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+z+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x+z+1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =z+1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int (z+1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =yz+y+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=yz+y+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy+x+yz+y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y+1 & =y+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =1 \\ h(z) & =z+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy+yz+x+y+z+C.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Radius of Curvature of a Plane Curve Given in Parametric Form
questions.problem: Find the radius of the curvature for the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{2t},\,{e}^{-t}⟩$ at $t=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)={e}^{2t},\,y(t)={e}^{-t}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =2{e}^{2t},\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-{e}^{-t} \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =4{e}^{2t},\, & {y}^{″}(t) & ={e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|2{e}^{2t}\cdot {e}^{-t}-(-{e}^{-t})\cdot 4{e}^{2t}|}{{((2{e}^{2t})^{2}+(-{e}^{-t})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{6{e}^{t}}{{(4{e}^{4t}+{e}^{-2t})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{6{e}^{(0)}}{{(4{e}^{4(0)}+{e}^{-2(0)})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{5}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{5\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{1}{κ(0)}=\frac{5\sqrt{5}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following is a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5$ for the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 5\end{aligned}]?
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following results:*

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-5I)^{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,(A-5I)^{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda ,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $k$ is a vector $v$ that satisfies

$$
(A-\lambda I)^{k}v=0\,\text{and}\,(A-\lambda I)^{k-1}v\ne 0.
$$

To find a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ corresponding to $\lambda =5,$ we need to find a vector $v$ that satisfies

$$
(A-5I)^{3}v=0\,\text{and}\,(A-5I)^{2}v\ne 0.
$$

Let's consider each condition:

- We start by solving $(A-5I)^{3}v=0.$ We're given that

$$
(A-5I)^{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\,.
$$

This means that *any* vector in ${R}^{3}$ is a solution to $(A-5I)^{3}v=0.$ Therefore, the solution to $(A-5I)^{3}v=0$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}v=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{2} \\ {v}_{3}\end{aligned}]={v}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{v}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{v}_{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we solve $(A-5I)^{2}v=0.$ We have

$$
(A-5I)^{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\,.
$$

This means that the solution to $(A-5I)^{2}v=0$ is ${v}_{1}=0,$ where ${v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ are free variables. Therefore, the solution to $(A-5I)^{2}v=0$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}v=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{2} \\ {v}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {v}_{2} \\ {v}_{3}\end{aligned}]={v}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{v}_{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the solutions, we see that the vector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ satisfies $(A-5I)^{3}v=0$ but does *not* satisfy $(A-5I)^{2}v=0.$ 

Hence, $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ of $A.$

questions.problem:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The position of the particle $y(t)$ at time $t$ is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+16y=32t.
$$

Which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for $y(t)?$

- $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡4t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+8t$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R$ and $ϕ$ are constants.

The general solution is the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution:

$$
y(t)={y}_{c}(t)+{y}_{p}(t)
$$

First, we find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(t),$ which is the solution to the simple harmonic motion equation ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=0.$ It can be written in three different forms:

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t$

In our case

$$
{\omega }^{2}=16\,⟹\,\omega =4.
$$

Thus, we have:

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡4t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡4t$

Next, we find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t).$ Since the external force is a linear function, we assume that the particular solution is also a linear function,

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha t+\beta .
$$

By substituting the particular solution into the differential equation and equating coefficients, we find that $\alpha =2$ and $\beta =0.$ So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=2t.
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+2t, \\ y(t) & =R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+2t, \\ y(t) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡4t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡4t+2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Only II matches the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

questions.problem:
Consider the following differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}+5y=x{e}^{2x}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)={e}^{2x}\,(A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+g(x),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following results (integration constants omitted):*

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x+x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ using the ansatz

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ satisfy the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
{u}_{1}(x)=-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,\,{u}_{2}(x)=\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,
$$

where $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is $f(x)=x{e}^{2x}.$

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)={e}^{2x}\,(A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x).
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are linearly independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}(x){y}_{2}^{′}(x)-{y}_{1}^{′}(x){y}_{2}(x) \\  & =({e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)({e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}-({e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}({e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =({e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-(2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)({e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{4x}({cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{4x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent.

Let’s compute ${u}_{1}(x)$ and ${u}_{2}(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx \\  & =-\int \frac{x{e}^{2x}\cdot {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{e}^{4x}}\,dx \\  & =-\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & =-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx \\  & =\int \frac{x{e}^{2x}\cdot {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{e}^{4x}}\,dx \\  & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x+x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =(x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)({e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)({e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{2x}\,(x{cos}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+x{sin}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =x{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & ={e}^{2x}\,(A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+{{x{e}^{2x}}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x)=x{e}^{2x}.
$$

Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

$\omega =2.$

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+ϕ)$

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)).
$$

$$

- $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)+\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

- $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Solutions I, II, and III match the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III".

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\frac{x{y}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is enclosed between two circles centered at $O$ of radii $4$ and $6,$ as shown above.

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents the annulus between the disks of radii $4$ and $6$ centered at the origin. 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16,$ we obtain $r=4.$

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36,$ we obtain $r=6.$

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,4\le r\le 6,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{x{y}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{4}^{6}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{4}^{6}\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {[r]}_{4}^{6}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (6-4)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{[\frac{{sin}^{3}⁡\theta }{3}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =5, & \,{f}^{′}(0,0) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(0,0) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(2,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =5, & \,\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}], & \,\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈5+[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,2) & ≈5+[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =5+[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =5+6+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}12 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =11+\frac{1}{2}(44) \\  & =33.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Variance of a Transformed Random Variable
questions.problem:
The probability distribution of the random variable $X$ is given below. Given that $\text{E}[X]=0,$ calculate $\text{Var}[\sqrt{5}X+4].$ 

| $x$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ | $\frac{3}{5}$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constants $a$ and $b,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[aX+b]={a}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=\sqrt{5}$ and $b=4.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\sqrt{5}X+4] & ={(\sqrt{5})}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =5\cdot \text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

Additionally, we're given that $\text{E}[X]=0.$ 

We start by computing $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & =(-1)^{2}\cdot f(-1)+{0}^{2}\cdot f(0)+{1}^{2}\cdot f(1) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}-{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\sqrt{5}X+4] & =5\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =5\cdot \frac{2}{5} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving for an Unknown Conditional Probability
questions.problem:
A local newspaper is sold by three distributors, $1,$ $2,$ and $3.$

- Distributor $1$ gets $36%$ of the copies.

- Distributor $2$ gets $23%$ of the copies, and $92%$ of those copies are sold.

- Distributor $3$ gets $41%$ of the copies, and $95%$ of those copies are sold.

If $3%$ of all copies have some printing defect, $70%$ of defective copies are sold, and $2.5%$ of sold copies are defective, what is the probability that a randomly chosen copy bought by distributor $1$ is sold? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the event that a copy has a printing defect, $S$ be the event that a copy is sold, and ${D}_{1},{D}_{2},{D}_{3}$ be the event that a copy is given to distributor $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively.

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({D}_{1})=0.36 \\  & P({D}_{2})=0.23 &  & P(S|{D}_{2})=0.92 \\  & P({D}_{3})=0.41 &  & P(S|{D}_{3})=0.95\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${D}_{1}⊔{D}_{2}⊔{D}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({D}_{1})+P({D}_{2})+P({D}_{3})=0.36+0.23+0.41=1.
$$

- Since $3%$ of all copies has some printing defect, we have

$$
P(R)=0.03.
$$

- Since $70%$ of defective copies are sold, we have

$$
P(S|R)=0.7.
$$

- Since $2.5%$ of sold copies are defective, we have

$$
P(R|S)=0.025.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen copy bought by distributor $1$ is sold, which is represented as $P(S|{D}_{1}).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R|S) & =\frac{P(S|R)P(R)}{P(S)} \\ P(R|S) & =\frac{P(S|R)P(R)}{P(S|{D}_{1})P({D}_{1})+P(S|{D}_{2})P({D}_{2})+P(S|{D}_{3})P({D}_{3})} \\ 0.025 & =\frac{(0.7)(0.03)}{P(S|{D}_{1})(0.36)+(0.92)(0.23)+(0.95)(0.41)} \\ 0.025 & =\frac{0.021}{0.36P(S|{D}_{1})+0.6011}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(S|{D}_{1}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.025(0.36P(S|{D}_{1})+0.6011) & =0.021 \\ 0.36P(S|{D}_{1})+0.6011 & =\frac{0.021}{0.025} \\ 0.36P(S|{D}_{1})+0.6011 & =\frac{21}{25} \\ 0.36P(S|{D}_{1}) & =\frac{21}{25}-0.6011 \\ P(S|{D}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{0.36}(\frac{21}{25}-0.6011) \\ P(S|{D}_{1}) & ≈0.664\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance Between Two Objects
questions.problem:
The gravitational force between two objects, of masses $(4.5\times {10}^{6})\,\text{kg}$ and $(2.8\times {10}^{6})\,\text{kg},$ has a magnitude of $(3.6\times {10}^{-3})\,\text{N}.$
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, what is the distance between the centers of mass of the two objects? Write your answer in scientific notation, rounding to **two significant figures** where appropriate. Assume the Newtonian constant of gravitation is $G=(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\,{\text{m}}^{3}/(\text{kg}\cdot {\text{s}}^{2}).$

The distance between the two objects is
$(${{field-1}}
$\times $
{{field-2}}$)\,\text{m}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Newton's law of universal gravitation states that the gravitational force attracting two objects is proportional to the product of the two masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers of mass:

$$
F=G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

where

- $F$ is the gravitational force between the objects, measured in Newtons $(\text{N}),$

- $G=(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\,{\text{m}}^{3}/(\text{kg}\cdot {\text{s}}^{2})$ is the Newtonian constant of gravitation,

- ${m}_{1}$ and ${m}_{2}$ are the masses of the objects, measured in $\text{kg},$ and

- $r$ is the distance between their centers of mass, measured in $\text{m}.$

First, let's rearrange the formula to make $r$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{2}} \\ {r}^{2} & =G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{F} \\ r & =\sqrt{G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{F}}\end{aligned}
$$

Choosing ${m}_{1}=(4.5\times {10}^{6})\,\text{kg}$ and ${m}_{2}=(2.8\times {10}^{6})\,\text{kg}$ and substituting in the other known values, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{2} & =(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\cdot \frac{(4.5\times {10}^{6})\cdot (2.8\times {10}^{6})}{3.6\times {10}^{-3}} \\  & =\frac{6.67\cdot 4.5\cdot 2.8}{3.6}\times \frac{{10}^{-11}\cdot {10}^{6}\cdot {10}^{6}}{{10}^{-3}} \\  & =23.345\times {10}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the square root, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{23.345\times {10}^{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{23.345}\times \sqrt{{10}^{4}} \\  & =(4.8316…)\times {10}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounded to two significant figures, the distance between the two objects is
$(\,4.8\times {10}^{2}\,)\,\text{m}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Conditional Probability Using the Law of Total Probability
questions.problem: Three baskets, $A,B,$ and $C,$ contain pears. It is known that $\frac{1}{6}$ of the pears from basket $A$ and $\frac{1}{5}$ of those from basket $B$ are ripe. A basket is selected at random, and a pear is chosen at random from the basket. If the probability that the selected pear is ripe is $\frac{1}{4},$  what proportion of the pears from basket $C$ are ripe?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the event that the pear is ripe, and

- let $A$ be the event that the pear comes from basket $A,$

- let $B$ be the event that the pear comes from basket $B,$

- let $C$ be the event that the pear comes from basket $C.$

Then the disjoint union $A⊔B⊔C$ covers the entire sample space.

To calculate the probability of selecting a ripe pear, we can use the law of total probability: 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R) & =P(R\cap A)+P(R\cap B)+P(R\cap C) \\  & =P(R|A)P(A)+P(R|B)P(B)+P(R|C)P(C)\end{aligned}
$$

Let's go through the problem statement and translate each piece of information into mathematical notation.

- Since a basket is selected at random, we have

$$
P(A)=P(B)=P(C)=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

- Since the probability of picking a ripe pear from baskets $A$ and $B$ are $\frac{1}{6}$ and $\frac{1}{5},$ respectively, we have

$$
P(R|A)=\frac{1}{6},\,P(R|B)=\frac{1}{5}
$$

- Since the probability of picking a ripe pear from one of the baskets is $\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
P(R)=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Substituting the above information into the law of total probability and solving for $P(R|C),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R) & =P(R|A)P(A)+P(R|B)P(B)+P(R|C)P(C) \\ \frac{1}{4} & =(\frac{1}{6})(\frac{1}{3})+(\frac{1}{5})(\frac{1}{3})+P(R|C)(\frac{1}{3}) \\ \frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{18}+\frac{1}{15}+\frac{1}{3}\cdot P(R|C) \\ \frac{1}{3}\cdot P(R|C) & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{18}-\frac{1}{15} \\ \frac{1}{3}\cdot P(R|C) & =\frac{23}{180} \\ P(R|C) & =\frac{23}{60}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{23}{60}$ of the pears from basket $C$ are ripe.

questions.problem:
In a particular city, about $30%$ of mornings are cloudy and $40%$ of days are rainy. 
It is known that $60%$ of rainy days start with cloudy mornings. What is the probability that a randomly selected cloudy morning continues as a rainy day?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be the event that a randomly selected morning is cloudy, and let $R$ be the event that a randomly selected day is rainy. Then, we require $P(R|C),$ which we can compute using Bayes' theorem.

$$
P(R|C)=\frac{P(C|R)P(R)}{P(C)}
$$

- $P(C)=0.3,$ since $30%$ of mornings are cloudy.

- $P(R)=0.4,$ since $40%$ of days are rainy.

- $P(C|R)=0.6,$ since $60%$ of rainy days start with cloudy mornings.

Therefore, using Bayes' theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R|C) & =\frac{P(C|R)P(R)}{P(C)} \\  & =\frac{0.6\cdot 0.4}{0.3} \\  & =0.8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing 4x4 Determinants Using Row and Column Operations
questions.problem:
Calculate the value of 
$\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & -3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 & -2 & 4 \\ -2 & -2 & 3 & 2\end{aligned}|.$

*Hint: Use elementary row operations to make the entries below ${a}_{12}$ equal to zero. You should be able to reduce the given $4\times 4$ determinant to a $3\times 3$ determinant.*
questions.worked_solution:
Using elementary row operations, let's make entries below ${a}_{12}=2$ equal to zero.

Since adding a multiple of one row (or column) to another row (column) in a matrix does not change the value of its determinant, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & -3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 & -2 & 4 \\ -2 & -2 & 3 & 2\end{aligned}| &  & \,\begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the result along the $2$nd column, we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+2}|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 \\ -4 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 \\ -4 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-2)\cdot 1\cdot (-1)^{2+2}|\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(4-3) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Subspaces of Function Vector Spaces
questions.problem:
Consider the vector space $C[-1,1]$ of all continuous functions $f:[-1,1]\to R$ and its subset $A={f\in C[-1,1]\,|\,f(1)\le 0}.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

- $A$ is closed under function addition
- $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- $A$ is a subspace of $C[-1,1]$
- $A$ is **not** a subspace of $C[-1,1]$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If $f(x),g(x)\in A,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}(f+g)(1) & =f(1)+g(1)\le 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $A$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is false. For example, if $f(x)\in A$ and $k=-1\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & \le 0 \\ kf(1) & \ge k\cdot 0 \\ (kf) & \ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $A$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $A$ is *not* a subspace because it's not closed under scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and IV only."

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Image of a Vector Given With Respect to the Standard Basis Under a Linear Map
questions.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B|C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -5 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 10\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ (shown above) and a basis $C$ of ${R}^{3}.$
The matrix $[T]_{B|C}$ of the linear map $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{3}$ relative to these bases, and the vector $x\in {R}^{2},$ are also given. Find $[T(x)]_{C}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the coordinates of the image of $x$ under $T$ relative to the basis $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $[x]_{B},$ the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B.$ So, let

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 10\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

This gives us the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-5 \\ 3{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=10.\end{aligned}
$$

We now row-reduce the corresponding augmented matrix using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -5 \\ 3 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 3 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}].$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -5 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -10 \\ -10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Projection of the Intersection of a Surface and a Tilted Plane
questions.problem: Find the projection of the intersection between the ellipsoid $\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{6}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{12}=1$ and the plane $z-y=3$ onto the $xy$-plane.
questions.worked_solution:
Since we want to find the projection onto the $xy$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $z.$ First, we solve the equation of the plane for $z$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-y=3\,⟹\,z=y+3\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the expression for $z$ into the equation of the ellipsoid, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{6}+\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{12} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{6}+\frac{{y}^{2}+6y+9}{12} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{3}+\frac{2{y}^{2}}{12}+\frac{{y}^{2}+6y+9}{12} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{3}+\frac{3{y}^{2}+6y+9}{12} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}+2y+3}{4} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by completing the square for the variable $y$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}+2y+3}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{3}+\frac{({y}^{2}+2y+1)+2}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{3}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}+2}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{3}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4}+\frac{1}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{3}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{2(x-2)^{2}}{3}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{3/2}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the projection of the intersection is the ellipse $\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{3/2}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{2}=1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Trajectories of a One-Parameter Family
questions.problem: Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family of curves $xy=C,$ where $C$ and $K$ are parameters.
questions.worked_solution:
Orthogonal trajectories are families of curves that intersect another given family of curves at right angles. In other words, the tangent lines of curves from each family are perpendicular at every intersection point.

Let's determine the slope of the family of curves given by $xy=C.$ First, we implicitly differentiate with respect to $x$ and solve for the derivative of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(xy) & =\frac{d}{dx}(C) \\ y+x{y}^{′} & =0 \\ x{y}^{′} & =-y \\ {y}^{′} & =-\frac{y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the parameter $C$ has already been eliminated.

For a curve to intersect this family orthogonally, its slope ${y}_{⊥}^{′}$ must be the negative reciprocal of the slope ${y}^{′}$ above. Hence,

$$
{y}_{⊥}^{′}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{′}}=-\frac{1}{(-\frac{y}{x})}=\frac{x}{y}.
$$

Hence, the orthogonal trajectories must satisfy

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x}{y}.
$$

To find the general solution, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y\cdot \frac{dy}{dx} & =x \\ \int y\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}\,dx & =\int x\,dx \\ \int y\,dy & =\int x\,dx \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{K}_{1} \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+K\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K=2{K}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

Therefore, the orthogonal trajectories of the family of curves $xy=C,$ where $C$ is a parameter, are given by

$$
{y}^{2}={x}^{2}+K,
$$

where $K$ is a parameter. Some curves from each family for specific parameter values are given in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14070542/assets/98159dfb60fd280468ad8165475b5ba58e41658174a932b4c9555ef1153a577c.png)

**Note**: For the slopes ${y}^{′}$ and ${y}_{⊥}^{′},$ we divide by $x$ and $y,$ respectively. So, the orthogonal trajectories are only defined on the region $x,y\ne 0.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order ODE Using a Substitution
questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation.

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}={y}^{2}-y
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution* $z={y}^{-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-1}\,⟹\,y={z}^{-1}\,
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ with the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}-\frac{1}{z} \\ -\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-z\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-1+z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-z & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-1,\,Q(x)=-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{-x}$ yields:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-x}\cdot (\frac{dz}{dx}-z) & ={e}^{-x}\cdot (-1) \\ {e}^{-x}\frac{dz}{dx}-{e}^{-x}z & =-{e}^{-x} \\ \frac{d}{dx}(z{e}^{-x}) & =-{e}^{-x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(z{e}^{-x})\,dx\, & =-\int {e}^{-x}\,dx \\ z{e}^{-x} & ={e}^{-x}+C \\ z & =1+C{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =1+C{e}^{x} \\ y & =\frac{1}{1+C{e}^{x}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Cases Where Differentiating Under the Integral Sign Applies
questions.problem:
For which of the following functions is it valid to differentiate under the integral sign?

- ${F}_{1}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+tx)}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (-1,1)$
- ${F}_{2}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{x-t}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (1,2)$
- ${F}_{3}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{|x-t|}}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (0,1)$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*

With that in mind, let's check each function:

- For the first function, we have 

$$
{f}_{1}(x,t)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+tx)}{1+{x}^{2}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (-1,1)$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(-1,1)$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{1}$ is continuous on $R$ (since $1+tx>0$). Computing the  partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂t}=\frac{x}{(1+tx)(1+{x}^{2})}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{1}^{′}(t)$ for all $t\in (-1,1).$

- For the second function, we have 

$$
{f}_{2}(x,t)=\frac{1}{x-t}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (1,2)$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(1,2)$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{2}$ is continuous on $R$ (since the denominator never vanishes on $R$). Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t}=\frac{1}{(x-t)^{2}},
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{2}^{′}(t)$ for all $t\in (1,2).$

- For the third function, we have 

$$
{f}_{3}(x,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|x-t|}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (0,1)$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(0,1)$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that this function is undefined when $x=t,$ since the denominator vanishes. Thus, ${f}_{3}$ is not continuous on $R,$ and differentiating under the integral sign is *not* valid.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.knowledge_point: Using Abel's Identity to Conclude Independence/Dependence
questions.problem:
$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}{y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0
$$

Let ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ be solutions to the second-order homogeneous differential equation above, where $Q(x)$ is continuous on $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ The Wronskian satisfies $W(0)=2.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.
The Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies the following first-order differential equation:

$$
{W}^{′}(x)={{field-1}}W(x)
$$

Solving this equation, we get

$$
W={{field-2}}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Now, using the fact that $W(0)=2,$ we obtain 
{{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Abel's identity says that if ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,
$$

then their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-P(x)W(x).
$$

In our equation, the coefficient of ${y}^{′}$ is 

$$
P(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Substituting into Abel's identity gives

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}W(x).
$$

Now, we solve the first-order differential equation for $W:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}W \\ \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =\int -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|W| & =-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+K \\ |W| & ={e}^{K}{e}^{-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)} \\ W & =C{e}^{-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Next, we use the given value $W(0)=2$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(0) & =C{e}^{-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)} \\ 2 & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have $W(x)\ne 0\text{ for all }x\in R.$

choices.value: $W(x)=0$ for some but not all $x\in R$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding Linear Transformations in the Cartesian Plane
questions.problem:
Consider a linear transformation $T$ that maps ${R}^{2}$ onto  ${R}^{2}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $\text{Im}(T)={0}$
- $\text{Ker}(T)={0}$
- $\text{nullity}(T)=1$, where $T$ is the standard matrix of $T$

Recall that a linear transformation $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto  ${R}^{2}$ if and only if 

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=2
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-2 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. The condition $\text{rank}(T)=2$ in ${R}^{2}$ is equivalent to

$$
\text{Im}(T)={R}^{2}.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the condition $\text{nullity}(T)=0$ in ${R}^{2}$ is equivalent to 

$$
\text{Ker}(T)={0}.
$$

- Statement III is false. We have that 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(4-x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14070542/assets/d4e5b78932f8ff6155ac81e12538eb31ac211c9d27d6a2b0c67542527ccd3b2a.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(4-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4-x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4-x & =0 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=4\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,4)$ | $4$ | $(4,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $2$ |  | $6$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $2>0$ | $0$ | $-2<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=4\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4-x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (4-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=4x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=6\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(6)^{2} & =4(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+18 \\ {v}^{2} & =8x-{x}^{2}+36 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-{x}^{2}+8x+36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+8x+36}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(4)=\sqrt{-(4)^{2}+8(4)+36}=2\sqrt{13}\,m/s
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inhibited Growth Model
questions.problem:
The volume $X(t)$ (in $\text{L}$) of water in a container as it fills toward its maximum capacity can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\frac{dX}{dt}=0.4(3-X),
$$

where $t\ge 0$ is the time, measured in minutes. If the initial volume is $1.5\,\text{L},$ how long does it take for the container to reach a volume of $2\,\text{L}?$ Round your answer to the nearest integer.
questions.worked_solution:
We're told that the container's volume is modeled by the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dX}{dt}=0.4(3-X).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dX}{3-X} & =0.4\,dt \\ \int \frac{dX}{3-X} & =\int 0.4\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-X| & =0.4t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $3-X>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$
Next, we solve for $X(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3-X & ={e}^{-0.4t-C} \\ 3-X & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-0.4t} \\ 3-X & =K{e}^{-0.4t} \\ X & =3-K{e}^{-0.4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the initial volume was $1.5\,\text{L}.$ So, we apply the initial condition $X(0)=1.5,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1.5 & =3-K{e}^{0} \\ 1.5 & =3-K \\ K & =1.5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
X(t)=3-1.5{e}^{-0.4t}.
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the volume is $2\,\text{L}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}X({t}_{1}) & =2 \\ 3-1.5{e}^{-0.4{t}_{1}} & =2 \\ 1 & =1.5{e}^{-0.4{t}_{1}} \\ {e}^{-0.4{t}_{1}} & =\frac{2}{3} \\ -0.4{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{3}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{0.4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =1.013… \\  & ≈1\,\text{minute},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Using the Invertible Matrix and Rank-Nullity Theorems
questions.problem:
If $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A+8I)=2,$ which of the following statements are true?

- $A+8I$ is singular
- $\lambda =-8$ is an eigenvalue of $A$
- $\text{rank}(A+8I)=2$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a $3\times 3$ matrix $M,$ we have the following by the invertible matrix theorem:

$M$ is invertible $\,⇔\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(M)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(M))=3=\text{rank}(M) \\  & \text{Null}(M)={0} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(M))=0=\text{nullity}(M)\end{aligned}$

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $M$ has $3$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(M)+\text{nullity}(M)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statements I is true. By the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{nullity}(A+8I)\ne 0,$ we obtain that $A+8I$ must be singular.

- Statement II is true. Notice that if $M=A+8I$ is singular, then $(A+8I)x=0$ has nonzero solutions which will be eigenvectors of $A.$ As a result, $\lambda =-8$ is an eigenvalue of $A.$

- Statement III is false. According to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A+8I) & =3-\text{nullity}(A+8I) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Carrying Capacity of a Logistic Growth Model In Context
questions.problem:
The population $y(t)$ of Weddell seals in a certain region of Antarctica follows the logistic growth model

$$
{y}^{′}=1.2y-0.002{y}^{2},\,y(0)=100,
$$

where $t$ is the time, in years. According to this model, what is the maximum possible seal population?
questions.worked_solution:
A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
{y}^{′}=ky(a-y),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>y$ is the carrying capacity. 

The carrying capacity $a$ represents the maximum possible population. A diagram showing a typical logistic growth curve is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14070542/assets/57f4b604c546daed4f1cb3895191fae0ccac33b5c17aac705f203f0a837c7e69.png)

First, let's rewrite the right-hand side of the given equation so that it matches the form above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =1.2y-0.002{y}^{2} \\  & =0.002y(600-y)\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we see that $a=600.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $600,$ and we conclude that the number of seals cannot exceed $600.$

questions.knowledge_point: Restoring a Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
questions.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $G$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $G,$ then $G$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $G=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $G,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
G={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}G & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-16 & 9 \\ -30 & 17\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Two Linearly Independent Complex Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
questions.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1-3\text{i} & 5 \\ -2 & 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-1-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-3\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{1}{5}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ \frac{1}{5}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1+3\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the  complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=-3\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(5)(5)}{(1+3\text{i})(1-3\text{i})}=\frac{5}{2}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Swapping the Order of Integration on a Non-Partitioned Region
questions.problem:
Change the order of integration in the double integral 
${\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{x-2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14070542/assets/75f9c68145ed74a2c3530012061eb65cd93bae38d82fa0d34e5dc042f8073841.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le x-2}.
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y=x-2\,⟹\,x=y+2
$$

and the right boundary of the region is

$$
x=4.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type II region. The type II representation of the region is

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,y-2\le x\le 4},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14070542/assets/575e7e482f88635f6267405f66857a5488dac79833fce16d3d998df19e24d119.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{x-2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y+2}^{4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Curl of a Vector Field Using the Product Rule
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨-1,0,x{y}^{3}⟩$ and the scalar field $f(x,y,z)=yz.$ Given that

$$
∇\times F=⟨3x{y}^{2},-{y}^{3},0⟩,\,∇f=⟨0,z,y⟩,
$$

calculate $∇\times (f\,F)$ at the point $(0,-1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
We shall use the following identity:

$$
∇\times (f\,F)=f∇\times F+∇f\times F
$$

First, we compute $∇f\times F.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f\times F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & z & y \\ -1 & 0 & x{y}^{3}\end{aligned}| \\  & =[z(x{y}^{3})-y(0)]i-[0(x{y}^{3})-y(-1)]j+[0(0)-z(-1)]k \\  & =xz{y}^{3}\,i-y\,j+z\,k \\  & =⟨xz{y}^{3},-y,z⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F) & =f∇\times F+∇f\times F \\  & =yz⟨3x{y}^{2},-{y}^{3},0⟩+⟨xz{y}^{3},-y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨3xz{y}^{3},-z{y}^{4},0⟩+⟨xz{y}^{3},-y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨4xz{y}^{3},-z{y}^{4}-y,z⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F)(0,-1,2) & =⟨4(0)(2)(-1)^{3},-2(-1)^{4}-(-1),2⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-1,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Hessian Determinant
questions.problem:
Given that 
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4xy-3{y}^{2} & 2{x}^{2}-6xy\end{aligned}],$ 
evaluate the Hessian determinant of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det(\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since
$\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4xy-3{y}^{2} & 2{x}^{2}-6xy\end{aligned}],$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4xy-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}-6xy.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy-3{y}^{2})=4y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-6xy)=4x-6y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy-3{y}^{2})=4x-6y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-6xy)=-6x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4y & 4x-6y \\ 4x-6y & -6x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(1,1)=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,1)=4\cdot (-6)-(-2)\cdot (-2)=-28.
$$
